method: Thermal conductivity is a material property measured in watts per metre-kelvin. Every listed unit is reduced to that SI base by one exact factor: watt per metre-kelvin is 1, milliwatt is 0.001, kilowatt is 1000, watt per centimetre-degree Celsius is 100, and the calorie-based units use the thermochemical calorie of exactly 4.184 J, so cal/(s·cm·°C) is 418.4 W/(m·K) and kcal/(h·m·°C) is 4184/3600 W/(m·K). The Btu units use the International Table Btu of exactly 1055.05585262 J, 3600 s per hour, 0.3048 m per foot, 0.0254 m per inch and a temperature interval of 5/9 K per °F: Btu/(h·ft·°F) is 1.73073466637 W/(m·K) and Btu·in/(h·ft²·°F) is 0.144227888864 W/(m·K). A conversion multiplies by the source factor and divides by the target factor, so every pair round trips. Input is trimmed and must be a plain decimal, optionally with grouped thousands; a leading decimal point is accepted, an exponent form is refused, and values below zero or above 1,000,000 W/(m·K) are rejected with the reason. Results carry six significant digits with trailing zeros trimmed and thousands grouped. The reference table lists typical handbook conductivities near room temperature for pure metals, common alloys and dry insulants; it is a material property, not a U-value or R-value. Everything runs in the browser; nothing is uploaded, stored or sent anywhere.
